title: Chapter 6 Drill: Neuromuscular Junction and Muscle Disease

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has generalized myasthenia gravis with acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Chest imaging shows a normal-sized thymus with no mass. She is stable on prednisone but wants to know whether surgery could help. What does the best randomized evidence show for thymectomy in this situation?
options: Better clinical outcomes and a lower steroid requirement over three years
No change in disability but fewer hospital admissions for pneumonia
Remission in all patients within six months of operation
Benefit only when a thymoma is confirmed pathologically
items.explanation: A randomized trial of extended transsternal thymectomy in nonthymomatous, receptor antibody positive generalized myasthenia under age 65 showed improved clinical scores and a reduced need for prednisone and other immunotherapy. The benefit accrues gradually, not by six months, and it is not universal remission. Thymoma is a separate indication for surgery, but thymectomy also helps patients with a normal thymus in this defined group.

items.stem: A 16-year-old with limb-girdle weakness and a mutation in FKRP develops exertional dyspnea. Which systemic evaluation is most important?
options: Slit-lamp examination for cataracts and retinal disease
items.explanation: Dystroglycanopathies caused by FKRP defects can produce dilated cardiomyopathy and restrictive respiratory failure, sometimes out of proportion to limb weakness, so echocardiography and pulmonary function tests are essential. Cataracts are a feature of myotonic dystrophy, and colorectal and renal surveillance are not part of this disorder. Early referral to cardiology and pulmonology allows treatment before decompensation develops.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man who smokes reports four months of difficulty climbing stairs, dry mouth, and erectile dysfunction. Reflexes are absent but briefly return after he sustains a hand grip. Which feature of this syndrome is most characteristic?
options: Prominent ptosis and diplopia as the first symptoms
Strength improves briefly with sustained effort
Marked muscle pain with elevated creatine kinase
Cranial nerve involvement with pupillary dilation as the earliest sign
items.explanation: Lambert-Eaton syndrome produces proximal leg weakness, autonomic dysfunction such as dry mouth and impotence, and depressed reflexes that transiently improve after exercise as calcium accumulates in the terminal. Ocular signs are less prominent than in myasthenia, muscle pain and high creatine kinase suggest myositis, and early dilated pupils are more typical of botulism. Examination after sustained effort is therefore a simple bedside clue.

items.stem: A woman with a heteroplasmic mitochondrial DNA point mutation has an affected child. What is the pattern of inheritance, and how does the mutation load vary?
options: Maternal inheritance, with variable mutation load between children
Paternal inheritance, with an identical mutation load in every child
items.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA is passed almost exclusively through the oocyte, so only a mother transmits the mutation, and a heteroplasmic mutation is distributed unevenly to offspring through the mitochondrial bottleneck, producing variable severity among siblings. Paternal transmission is not seen, and the X-linked and autosomal dominant models do not describe this pattern. Genetic counseling should explain this variability.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a heliotrope rash, a violaceous rash over the upper back and shoulders, and proximal weakness. Antibody testing shows anti-Mi-2. Which clinical feature is most characteristic of this subtype?
options: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with respiratory failure
Florid skin disease with a relatively favorable response to treatment
Severe myopathy with minimal skin findings
items.explanation: Anti-Mi-2 antibodies are associated with classic dermatomyositis including shawl and V-sign rashes, cuticular overgrowth, and generally good responses to immunotherapy. Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease points to anti-MDA5, a high cancer risk to anti-TIF1 gamma or NXP2, and severe necrotizing myopathy with little rash to anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies. Antibody type therefore guides prognosis and screening.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has progressive proximal weakness, a creatine kinase of 2,000 U/L, and no rash. Muscle biopsy shows CD8 positive T cells surrounding and invading non-necrotic fibers, with MHC class I expression. Which condition does this support?
options: Polymyositis, or the inflammatory pattern that overlaps with inclusion body myositis
items.explanation: Endomysial CD8 positive T cell invasion of non-necrotic fibers with diffuse MHC class I expression defines the cytotoxic T-cell pattern of polymyositis. The same finding is frequent in inclusion body myositis, which is why the diagnosis requires scrutiny for rimmed vacuoles. Dermatomyositis shows perifascicular change, necrotizing myopathy shows necrosis with little inflammation, and congenital myopathy is genetic with distinctive structural findings.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman with newly diagnosed dermatomyositis has started high-dose prednisone. Which addition is most appropriate as a long-term steroid-sparing agent?
items.explanation: Corticosteroids are first-line in dermatomyositis, with an early steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine to allow tapering, and intravenous immune globulin reserved for refractory disease. Eculizumab targets complement in other disorders, pyridostigmine supports junction transmission and does nothing for inflammation, and interferon beta is a treatment for multiple sclerosis that can aggravate some inflammatory conditions.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a son with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. She has no weakness but her creatine kinase is mildly elevated. What is the most important clinical implication for her?
options: She is a carrier and needs periodic cardiac evaluation
She will certainly develop limb weakness by age 50
A normal creatine kinase would have excluded carrier status
items.explanation: Carriers of dystrophin mutations may have elevated creatine kinase and, even without weakness, can develop dilated cardiomyopathy in adulthood, so periodic cardiac evaluation is advised. Skeletal weakness occurs in a minority and not inevitably. A normal creatine kinase does not exclude carrier status, and steroid treatment is not indicated for an asymptomatic carrier. Counseling about genetic testing for relatives is also appropriate.

items.stem: A 10-year-old girl has episodic flaccid weakness, low-set ears, a small chin, and fifth finger clinodactyly. Her electrocardiogram shows prominent U waves and ventricular ectopy. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Andersen-Tawil syndrome combines periodic paralysis, long QT interval with ventricular arrhythmias, and dysmorphic features from mutations in KCNJ2, which encodes the inward rectifier potassium channel. CACNA1S causes hypokalemic periodic paralysis, CLCN1 causes myotonia congenita, and SCN4A causes hyperkalemic periodic paralysis or paramyotonia. The arrhythmia risk makes cardiac evaluation essential. Electrocardiographic monitoring should be repeated over time.

items.stem: A 3-month-old girl has profound hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly with a short PR interval. Creatine kinase is elevated. Which treatment targets the underlying disorder?
options: Dietary carnitine supplementation combined with a high-protein and low-fat diet
Recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme replacement
items.explanation: Infantile-onset Pompe disease is a lysosomal glycogen storage disorder from acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, presenting with hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and macroglossia, and enzyme replacement started early improves survival and cardiac outcome. Carnitine supplementation treats carnitine transport defects, and immune globulin and immunosuppressants treat inflammatory or autoimmune disease, not a storage disorder. Treatment is most effective when it begins before irreversible muscle damage.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis is stable on mycophenolate mofetil and pyridostigmine. She tells you she plans to become pregnant within the year. Which change should be made before conception?
options: Stop all immunotherapy and continue only pyridostigmine
Add cyclophosphamide for stronger disease control
items.explanation: Mycophenolate is teratogenic and must be stopped well before conception, with azathioprine the usual compatible steroid-sparing replacement. Abruptly stopping all immunotherapy risks relapse or crisis. Methotrexate and cyclophosphamide are also contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal toxicity. Pyridostigmine can be continued, and planning the switch early lets disease stability be confirmed on the new agent.

items.stem: Botulinum toxin causes paralysis by acting at which step of neuromuscular transmission?
options: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
Impaired sodium channel inactivation in the muscle membrane
Cleavage of SNARE proteins needed for acetylcholine vesicle fusion
items.explanation: The toxin light chain is a zinc protease that cleaves SNARE proteins such as SNAP-25 or synaptobrevin, so acetylcholine vesicles cannot fuse and release transmitter. Postsynaptic receptor blockade describes curare and similar agents, acetylcholinesterase inhibition describes organophosphates, and impaired sodium channel inactivation underlies paramyotonia. This presynaptic action also explains the facilitation seen on high-frequency stimulation.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had slowly progressive weakness of quadriceps and wrist and finger flexors for several years, with dysphagia. Creatine kinase is mildly raised. Which biopsy finding best supports inclusion body myositis?
options: Central cores lacking oxidative enzyme activity
Group atrophy with fiber type grouping
items.explanation: Inclusion body myositis shows endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, and protein aggregates, and clinically it affects finger flexors and quadriceps, with poor response to immunosuppression. Perifascicular atrophy is seen in dermatomyositis, central cores in congenital myopathy, and group atrophy with fiber type grouping in denervating disease. Anti-cN1A antibody supports the diagnosis but lacks perfect sensitivity. Dysphagia occurs in a substantial fraction.

items.stem: A 7-year-old boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy has a deletion of exons 48 to 50. He is eligible for an exon 51 skipping antisense oligonucleotide. What is the intended molecular effect?
options: Replacing the entire dystrophin gene with a viral copy
Increasing utrophin transcription to replace dystrophin
Restoring the reading frame so a shortened functional dystrophin is made
Blocking myostatin to increase muscle mass
items.explanation: Deleting exons 48 to 50 shifts the reading frame and truncates dystrophin. Skipping exon 51 at the pre-mRNA stage restores the frame, producing a shortened dystrophin like that in Becker dystrophy, so the approach is mutation specific. Whole-gene replacement is not possible because of gene size, and utrophin upregulation and myostatin blockade are separate strategies that are not the mechanism of antisense oligonucleotides.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has an inclusion body myositis phenotype. Which autoantibody can support the diagnosis but does not exclude it when absent?
items.explanation: Antibodies to cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase 1A are found in a substantial proportion of inclusion body myositis patients and help support the diagnosis, but the test has limited sensitivity, so a negative result does not exclude it and the clinical and pathologic pattern remains decisive. Anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR identify necrotizing myopathy and anti-Jo-1 identifies antisynthetase syndrome. Pattern recognition remains central.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy is diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy after genetic testing. His parents ask about corticosteroids. Which statement best reflects current care?
options: Steroids are reserved for after loss of ambulation
Daily or intermittent glucocorticoids prolong ambulation and are usually started before motor decline
Steroids cure the dystrophin deficiency in most boys
Steroids should be avoided because they accelerate respiratory decline
items.explanation: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone or deflazacort slow the loss of strength, delay loss of ambulation, and reduce scoliosis and cardiopulmonary decline, and are generally begun in the ambulatory child before motor function declines, with attention to growth, bone health, and weight. They do not restore dystrophin and are not reserved for later disease. Evidence supports a respiratory benefit, not harm.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has myoclonic seizures, ataxia, progressive hearing loss, and a muscle biopsy showing ragged red fibers. Her mother has migraines and short stature. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Unverricht-Lundborg disease caused by a CSTB repeat expansion mutation
MERRF syndrome, due to the m.8344A>G mitochondrial DNA mutation
items.explanation: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disease combining myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia, hearing loss, and myopathy, most often from the m.8344A>G mutation. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy has no systemic features or ragged fibers, and Unverricht-Lundborg and Lafora diseases are autosomal recessive progressive myoclonus epilepsies with different pathology, without mitochondrial inheritance. Muscle biopsy supports the diagnosis.

items.stem: A male newborn has profound hypotonia, ventilator dependence, ptosis, and ophthalmoparesis. His mother has a mild proximal myopathy. Biopsy shows small fibers with central nuclei. Which gene is most likely mutated?
options: SMN1 encoding survival motor neuron protein
items.explanation: X-linked myotubular myopathy, caused by MTM1 mutation, presents in boys with severe neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure, and ophthalmoplegia, with fibers resembling fetal myotubes and central nuclei, while carrier mothers can be mildly affected. ACTA1 causes nemaline rod disease, SMN1 deficiency causes spinal muscular atrophy with preserved eye movements and without central nuclei, and COL6A1 causes Ullrich or Bethlem myopathy.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has had three years of fatigable ptosis and diplopia without limb or bulbar weakness. Pyridostigmine gives only partial relief, and the diplopia now interferes with her work. Which next step is most appropriate?
items.explanation: For ocular myasthenia that remains symptomatic on pyridostigmine, a low-dose corticosteroid is the usual next step and may also lower the chance of progression to generalized disease. Thymectomy is reserved for thymoma or selected generalized disease, maintenance plasma exchange is a rescue or bridging tool, and complement inhibition is held for refractory generalized disease, not isolated ocular symptoms.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man develops muscle pain and dark urine after a long run on an empty stomach and after a viral illness with fever. Between episodes he is well and strength is normal. Which defect is most likely?
items.explanation: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency causes episodic rhabdomyolysis triggered by prolonged exercise, fasting, cold, or fever, because long-chain fatty acid oxidation fails when glycogen is depleted, and the patient is normal between episodes. Myophosphorylase deficiency causes cramps with short intense exercise and a second wind, acid maltase deficiency causes progressive weakness, and dystrophin deficiency causes persistent weakness.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis refractory to standard therapy is about to begin eculizumab. Which preparatory step is required?
items.explanation: Terminal complement inhibition impairs defense against encapsulated Neisseria, so meningococcal vaccination (with prophylactic antibiotics considered if therapy cannot wait) is required before starting eculizumab or ravulizumab. Hepatitis A vaccination is not the relevant safeguard, a bone marrow biopsy is not required for this indication, and thymic radiotherapy has no role in preparing for complement inhibition.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and an episode of hypoketotic hypoglycemia after a gastrointestinal illness. Plasma free carnitine is very low. Which treatment is expected to help?
options: Prednisone at 1 mg per kg daily
items.explanation: Primary carnitine deficiency from impaired carnitine transport (OCTN2) presents with cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia, and high-dose carnitine can restore levels and reverse the cardiomyopathy. Potassium is for periodic paralysis, and prednisone or immune globulin are used for inflammatory disorders, which this metabolic disease is not. Lifelong supplementation with regular cardiac follow-up and glucose monitoring during illness is needed.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has new dermatomyositis with anti-TIF1 gamma antibodies. Which statement about her management is most accurate?
options: She needs a thorough, repeated search for an underlying malignancy
Malignancy screening is unnecessary after age 60
Treatment of the rash will treat any tumor
Cancer risk is lowest during the first year following the diagnosis of myositis
items.explanation: Anti-TIF1 gamma dermatomyositis in adults is strongly associated with cancer, most often ovarian, breast, lung, colon, and pancreatic, with risk highest around the time of diagnosis, so age-appropriate screening plus body imaging is repeated over the first years. Immunosuppression does not treat a tumor, and older age raises, not lowers, the importance of screening. Repeat imaging is considered if symptoms change.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has weakness, an elevated creatine kinase, and a brain MRI showing diffuse white matter T2 hyperintensity with normal cognition. Muscle biopsy shows absent laminin alpha-2 (merosin). Which diagnosis fits?
items.explanation: Merosin deficiency results from LAMA2 mutation and produces congenital hypotonia with a dystrophic biopsy, high creatine kinase, and characteristic white matter changes on MRI with generally preserved intellect. Duchenne dystrophy shows absent dystrophin and no white matter abnormality. Pompe disease is a lysosomal glycogen storage disorder, and spinal muscular atrophy causes neurogenic weakness with normal creatine kinase.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl develops unsteady gait followed by flaccid ascending weakness over 24 hours after a camping trip in the spring. Cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal and she has no sensory complaints. What is the most important next step?
options: Search the scalp and skin carefully for an attached tick
Start intravenous immune globulin immediately and admit to intensive care
items.explanation: Rapidly ascending flaccid paralysis with normal cerebrospinal fluid protein after outdoor exposure should prompt a full skin and scalp examination, because tick paralysis from a salivary neurotoxin resolves quickly after tick removal. Immune globulin and steroids are not indicated unless a tick is not found and another diagnosis is established. Muscle biopsy has no role in this acute presentation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has subacute severe proximal weakness with creatine kinase of 12,000 U/L, no rash, and no cancer. Muscle biopsy shows scattered necrotic fibers with minimal inflammation. Antibody testing is most likely to show which result?
items.explanation: Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is characterized by markedly elevated creatine kinase and necrotic fibers with little inflammation, and anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies are the two main markers. Anti-Jo-1 marks antisynthetase syndrome with lung disease, anti-cN1A marks inclusion body myositis, and receptor antibodies belong to myasthenia, which does not raise creatine kinase. Statin exposure history should also be asked.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with stable myasthenia gravis is admitted with a ventricular arrhythmia, and the team considers several new agents. Which agent should be avoided because it can precipitate myasthenic weakness?
options: Apixaban at the standard anticoagulation dose
items.explanation: Magnesium inhibits presynaptic acetylcholine release and reduces postsynaptic sensitivity, so intravenous magnesium can provoke weakness or crisis in myasthenia and should be avoided or used with great care. Apixaban, amlodipine, and levetiracetam have no meaningful junction-blocking effect. Other recognized offenders include aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, and beta-blockers. Recognizing these triggers lets the team choose safe alternatives before weakness appears in a patient with limited respiratory reserve.

items.stem: A 22-year-old athletic man abruptly develops difficulty standing on tiptoes, with atrophy of the gastrocnemius muscles. His creatine kinase is 50 times normal and muscle biopsy shows inflammatory cells. Steroids produce no benefit. Which gene is most likely mutated?
items.explanation: Dysferlinopathy, or limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2B, typically presents in young adulthood with calf weakness, markedly elevated creatine kinase, and biopsy inflammation that leads to misdiagnosis as polymyositis, with no steroid response. DMD causes dystrophin disease with earlier onset, EMD causes Emery-Dreifuss dystrophy with contractures and cardiac conduction disease, and PABPN1 causes oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Biopsy findings can therefore mislead clinicians.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy has brief attacks of flaccid weakness lasting less than two hours, typically after resting following vigorous exercise. Serum potassium is elevated during attacks, and he has mild eyelid myotonia. Which treatment approach is appropriate?
options: Oral potassium chloride during attacks, repeated hourly until strength returns
Carbohydrate in attacks, with acetazolamide or a thiazide as prevention
items.explanation: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis from SCN4A mutation causes brief attacks after rest following exercise, often with myotonia. Mild attacks are aborted with carbohydrate or inhaled beta-agonists, and prevention uses carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or thiazide diuretics, together with avoidance of potassium-rich food. Giving potassium is dangerous, and carbohydrate is a treatment rather than a trigger in this variant.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis has an anterior mediastinal mass on computed tomography. In addition to acetylcholine receptor antibodies, which antibody is commonly found when a thymoma is present?
items.explanation: Antibodies against titin and other striational proteins are frequent in thymoma-associated myasthenia and in late-onset disease, and a positive titer in a young patient should raise suspicion for thymoma. MuSK antibodies are typically mutually exclusive with receptor antibodies and not linked to thymoma. Anti-Hu is a paraneoplastic neuronal antibody and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase is associated with stiff person syndrome and cerebellar ataxia.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man with severe asthma has been in the intensive care unit for two weeks receiving high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone and a neuromuscular blocker. He cannot be weaned from the ventilator, has flaccid quadriparesis, and has normal sensation. Which finding is most expected?
options: Low amplitude motor responses with normal sensory responses and a normal or mildly raised creatine kinase
Absent sensory responses with markedly slow conduction velocity
Decrement on repetitive stimulation at 3 Hz
Markedly raised creatine kinase with anti-signal recognition particle antibody
items.explanation: Critical illness myopathy follows severe illness with corticosteroids and neuromuscular blockade, with selective loss of thick myosin filaments. Motor amplitudes fall, sensory responses are preserved, and creatine kinase is normal or modestly raised. Sensory loss with slow conduction suggests polyneuropathy, a decrement suggests a junction disorder, and a very high creatine kinase with antibody suggests immune necrotizing myopathy.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy is still walking. His echocardiogram is normal. Which cardiac strategy is recommended?
options: No cardiac surveillance until symptoms of heart failure appear
Annual cardiac imaging and starting an ACE inhibitor or similar agent by about age 10
items.explanation: Cardiomyopathy is nearly universal in Duchenne dystrophy by adulthood, and fibrosis develops before symptoms. Guidelines advise baseline and regular imaging, with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker begun by about age 10 even when function is normal, adding beta-blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists as needed. Waiting for symptoms is too late, and defibrillators or transplantation are not routine preventive steps.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman cannot whistle, sleeps with her eyes slightly open, and has marked asymmetric scapular winging. Her father had a similar condition. Which additional finding should be sought?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with early heart block and atrial arrhythmia
Retinal vascular telangiectasias and high-frequency hearing loss
items.explanation: Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is autosomal dominant with facial and scapular weakness, often asymmetric, and extramuscular features include Coats-like retinal telangiectasia and high-frequency hearing loss. Early heart block, baldness with testicular atrophy, and cognitive effects characterize myotonic dystrophy and other disorders. Cardiac involvement is uncommon in facioscapulohumeral dystrophy. Retinal screening is useful because severe vascular disease can threaten vision in some patients.

items.stem: During forearm exercise testing without ischemia in a patient with exertional cramps and myoglobinuria, venous ammonia rises normally but lactate does not rise. What does this pattern indicate?
options: A glycolysis block, such as myophosphorylase deficiency
A defect in long-chain fatty acid oxidation
A mitochondrial respiratory chain defect with excess lactate
items.explanation: A normal ammonia rise confirms that the patient exercised adequately, and failure of lactate to rise indicates blocked glycolysis or glycogenolysis, as in McArdle disease and other glycolytic defects. Normal metabolism would raise lactate, fatty acid oxidation defects have a normal lactate response, and mitochondrial disease typically gives an exaggerated lactate rise at low workload.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis is started on prednisone 60 mg daily as an outpatient. Five days later her swallowing is worse and she is short of breath. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Development of a second antibody-mediated syndrome
Adrenal insufficiency from the new steroid
items.explanation: Starting high-dose corticosteroids can briefly worsen myasthenia within the first one to two weeks, sometimes enough to cause crisis. This is why steroids are often begun at a low dose and increased gradually, or started in hospital with a rapid-acting therapy ready. A second syndrome, abrupt thymoma growth, and adrenal insufficiency do not fit the timing, and adrenal suppression follows prolonged use, not days.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man has episodic muscle weakness and pain, with lipid storage myopathy on biopsy, elevated organic acids, and abnormal acylcarnitine profile. Symptoms and biochemical abnormalities improve markedly after starting a vitamin. Which supplement is the most likely effective therapy?
items.explanation: Riboflavin-responsive multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (often from ETFDH mutation) causes lipid storage myopathy with fluctuating proximal weakness and a typical acylcarnitine profile, and many patients improve dramatically with riboflavin and coenzyme Q10. Thiamine treats Wernicke encephalopathy and certain mitochondrial presentations, vitamin K treats coagulopathy, and folic acid is for folate deficiency, none of which explains the biochemical pattern.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man who injects drugs subcutaneously presents with fever at an injection site abscess, followed by drooping eyelids, blurred vision, and descending weakness over two days. Pupils are sluggish and sensation is normal. Which pathogenic mechanism and management fits best?
options: Guillain-Barre syndrome, treated with plasma exchange
Wound botulism, treated with antitoxin and wound debridement
Myasthenic crisis, treated with immune globulin
items.explanation: Descending cranial and limb weakness with dilated or sluggish pupils and preserved sensation after skin injection points to wound botulism from Clostridium botulinum in infected tissue. Management includes wound debridement, antibiotics, and heptavalent antitoxin as early as possible. Tetanus causes rigidity and spasms, Guillain-Barre syndrome is ascending with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation, and myasthenia does not usually involve the pupils.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has mild skin disease with amyopathic features but progressive hypoxemia and a ground glass pattern on chest computed tomography. Which antibody is most likely?
items.explanation: Anti-MDA5 antibodies are linked to clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with skin ulceration and rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease that carries a high mortality, requiring urgent aggressive immunosuppression. Anti-Mi-2 predicts classic skin and muscle disease with good response, anti-TIF1 gamma predicts malignancy, and anti-cN1A is associated with inclusion body myositis rather than lung disease. Early recognition of this antibody is therefore urgent.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with generalized myasthenia gravis has had two days of worsening shortness of breath. He is anxious and speaking in short phrases, and his pulse oximetry is 97 percent on room air. Which measurement best identifies impending respiratory failure?
options: Serial forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force
Single measurement of arterial pH taken at the time of presentation
items.explanation: In neuromuscular respiratory failure, oxygen saturation stays normal until the patient is exhausted, so it is falsely reassuring. Serial forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force detect falling muscle strength early, and thresholds such as a vital capacity near 20 mL/kg or less guide intubation. Hypercapnia and acidosis are late findings, and respiratory rate alone is unreliable and easily affected by anxiety.

items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has slowly progressive weakness of the forearm extensors and neck, with repetitive compound muscle action potentials after a single stimulus on nerve conduction testing. Which treatment is expected to help?
items.explanation: A repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus with selective forearm extensor and neck weakness suggests slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome, a gain-of-function receptor channel disorder with prolonged open time. Open-channel blockers such as fluoxetine or quinidine shorten channel opening. Pyridostigmine worsens the excess depolarizing current, albuterol is used mainly in DOK7 and similar forms, and plasma exchange is ineffective because the cause is genetic, not antibody mediated.

items.stem: A 16-year-old has progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and an episode of syncope. Electrocardiography shows a new bifascicular block. What is the most important next management step?
options: Muscle biopsy before any other cardiac or diagnostic action
items.explanation: Kearns-Sayre syndrome, typically from a single large mtDNA deletion, includes ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and onset before age 20, and the major cause of death is progressive cardiac conduction block, so pacemaker evaluation is urgent when conduction disease appears. Steroids do not treat mitochondrial disease, biopsy can wait, and observation risks sudden death from complete heart block.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 120 mg every three hours develops abdominal cramps, diarrhea, excessive salivation, and widespread fasciculations. His weakness is also worse. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Typical presentation of myasthenic crisis needing a higher dose
Cholinergic excess from too much pyridostigmine
Early Lambert-Eaton syndrome from an occult tumor
items.explanation: Muscarinic symptoms (cramps, diarrhea, salivation) and fasciculations on a high dose of an anticholinesterase suggest cholinergic excess, which can paradoxically worsen weakness through depolarizing block. Raising the dose would deepen the problem. Lambert-Eaton syndrome and botulism may cause dry mouth or autonomic features of a different type, not salivation and fasciculations. Reducing the dose is the first step.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman with dermatomyositis undergoes muscle biopsy. Which histologic finding is most characteristic?
options: Endomysial CD8 positive T cells invading non-necrotic fibers
Ragged red fibers with cytochrome oxidase negative fibers
items.explanation: Dermatomyositis is a complement-mediated microangiopathy, and its hallmark is perifascicular atrophy with perivascular and perimysial inflammation, mostly B cells and CD4 positive T cells. Rimmed vacuoles characterize inclusion body myositis, endomysial CD8 invasion of non-necrotic fibers characterizes polymyositis and overlaps with inclusion body myositis, and ragged red fibers point to mitochondrial myopathy. Biopsy pattern is therefore a reliable discriminator.

items.stem: A 21-year-old man has stiffness and weakness of his hands and face when exposed to cold, and the stiffness worsens, not improves, with repeated activity. Which mutation is most likely?
items.explanation: Paramyotonia congenita is a skeletal muscle sodium channel disorder (SCN4A) with cold-induced myotonia that paradoxically worsens with exercise, in contrast to the warm-up pattern of chloride channel myotonia. DMPK expansion causes myotonic dystrophy with progressive weakness and systemic features, and KCNJ2 mutation causes Andersen-Tawil syndrome with periodic paralysis and arrhythmia. Cold exposure is the key history clue.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with fever, proximal weakness, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and shortness of breath has a positive anti-Jo-1 antibody. Which is the most important organ system to evaluate?
options: Lungs, using chest imaging and pulmonary function tests
Peripheral nerves, with sural nerve biopsy and nerve conduction studies
items.explanation: Antisynthetase syndrome combines myositis, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, fever, and mechanic's hands, and the lung disease often determines outcome, so early imaging and pulmonary function testing are essential. Renal, retinal, and peripheral nerve involvement are not core features and would not drive the first evaluation. Prompt detection allows early immunosuppression and may preserve lung function.

items.stem: A family eats home-canned vegetables, and two members develop nausea followed by dry mouth, double vision, and difficulty swallowing within 24 hours. Which finding most helps distinguish their illness from myasthenia gravis?
options: Painless weakness limited to extraocular muscles only
Sensory loss in a stocking distribution
Dilated, poorly reactive pupils with prominent dry mouth
items.explanation: Foodborne botulism begins with gastrointestinal symptoms and then produces symmetric descending cranial neuropathies with autonomic dysfunction, including dry mouth and poorly reactive pupils, because the toxin blocks cholinergic transmission at parasympathetic terminals as well. Myasthenia spares the pupils. Fatigable ptosis that improves with rest and restriction to extraocular muscles do not discriminate, and sensory loss is absent in botulism.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with severe preeclampsia is receiving a magnesium sulfate infusion. Her deep tendon reflexes disappear and her respiratory rate falls. After stopping the infusion, which intervention reverses the neuromuscular effects?
items.explanation: Hypermagnesemia blocks presynaptic calcium entry, reducing acetylcholine release, so reflexes are lost first and respiratory depression follows at higher levels. Calcium restores release and reverses the block. Pyridostigmine and atropine address cholinesterase and muscarinic effects, which are not the issue, and dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia and would only add weakness. Magnesium levels should be rechecked and renal function reviewed.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has severe thigh pain and swelling after a marathon, followed by dark urine. Creatine kinase is 85,000 U/L and creatinine is rising. Which immediate measure is most important?
options: Alkalinization with intravenous potassium bicarbonate infusion
items.explanation: In rhabdomyolysis the principal danger is pigment nephropathy and hyperkalemia, and early large-volume isotonic fluid resuscitation to maintain urine output is the cornerstone of care, with monitoring of potassium, calcium, and compartments. Steroids offer no benefit, potassium administration is dangerous when potassium is already rising, and muscle biopsy is deferred until the acute illness has resolved.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV infection has taken zidovudine for several years and develops progressive proximal weakness with myalgia. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated. Muscle biopsy is most likely to show which feature?
options: Ragged red fibers from mitochondrial toxicity
items.explanation: Zidovudine inhibits mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma and can cause a toxic mitochondrial myopathy, with ragged red fibers on Gomori trichrome and improvement after withdrawal. Perifascicular atrophy is the hallmark of dermatomyositis, rimmed vacuoles characterize inclusion body myositis, and rods characterize nemaline myopathy, so each corresponds to a different disease mechanism. Stopping the drug usually brings gradual recovery.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with MuSK antibody positive myasthenia gravis has severe neck, bulbar, and tongue weakness. A colleague suggests adding a complement inhibitor. What is the strongest argument against relying on this strategy in her disease?
options: MuSK antibodies are IgM and are cleared by the spleen
The pathogenic antibodies are mainly IgG4 and do not activate complement
Complement is depleted in all patients with bulbar weakness
items.explanation: MuSK myasthenia is mediated chiefly by IgG4 antibodies that disrupt the MuSK and LRP4 signaling needed to cluster receptors, and IgG4 is a poor activator of complement. That is why the rationale for complement blockade, which works in receptor antibody disease, does not carry over. The antibodies are not IgM, complement is not depleted by bulbar disease, and complement inhibitors have no cholinergic effect.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man of Asian descent wakes with severe flaccid quadriparesis. Serum potassium is 2.1 mmol/L, and he has tachycardia, tremor, and weight loss. What is the most important definitive treatment?
options: High-dose intravenous potassium bolus given rapidly until levels normalize
Treat the hyperthyroidism, with propranolol and antithyroid drugs
items.explanation: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is an acquired hypokalemic paralysis, most common in men of East Asian descent, driven by thyroid hormone excess and sodium-potassium pump overactivity. Treating the hyperthyroidism cures it, and propranolol helps acutely. Potassium replacement should be cautious because of rebound hyperkalemia, acetazolamide alone does not treat the cause, and plasma exchange has no role.

items.stem: A woman with myotonic dystrophy type 1 and mild symptoms gives birth to an infant with severe hypotonia, respiratory failure, and a tented upper lip. What explains the severity of the child's disease?
options: A new mitochondrial mutation arising in the oocyte
Loss of dystrophin from a deletion on the X chromosome
Acquired maternal antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor
Expansion of the CTG repeat across generations, most marked with maternal transmission
items.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is caused by a CTG expansion in DMPK that tends to lengthen in successive generations (anticipation), and congenital disease almost always follows maternal transmission of a large expansion. A mitochondrial mutation and dystrophin loss do not match the inheritance or phenotype. Maternal receptor antibodies cause transient neonatal myasthenia, which would not include the tented lip and would improve within weeks.

items.stem: A 9-year-old girl has difficulty rising from the floor, calf hypertrophy, and creatine kinase 20 times normal. Dystrophin immunostaining on muscle biopsy is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy with early onset weakness
items.explanation: A Duchenne-like phenotype in a girl with normal dystrophin staining suggests an autosomal recessive sarcoglycanopathy, which is part of the limb-girdle group and may involve the heart. Becker dystrophy would show abnormal dystrophin, and the X-linked pattern makes it unlikely in a girl. Facioscapulohumeral and oculopharyngeal dystrophies cause facial, scapular, ptotic, or swallowing weakness and are not typical in childhood.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the molecular pathogenesis of myotonic dystrophy type 1?
options: Loss of function of the dystrophin protein causing membrane fragility
Toxic RNA repeats sequester splicing proteins and cause missplicing of other transcripts
A point mutation in the skeletal muscle chloride channel
items.explanation: Expanded CUG repeats in the DMPK transcript form nuclear foci that sequester proteins of the MBNL family and upregulate CELF1, so many pre-mRNAs are mis-spliced; abnormal chloride channel splicing explains myotonia and insulin receptor missplicing explains insulin resistance. Dystrophin loss, a chloride channel point mutation (myotonia congenita), and mitochondrial defects are separate mechanisms. Understanding this explains the multisystem features.

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl with juvenile dermatomyositis develops painful firm subcutaneous nodules that discharge chalky material. Antibody testing is most likely to identify which antibody?
items.explanation: Calcinosis is a hallmark complication of juvenile dermatomyositis and is particularly associated with anti-NXP2 antibodies, which in adults also link to malignancy. Anti-Mi-2 identifies classic skin-predominant dermatomyositis with good prognosis, anti-Ro52 is a nonspecific accompanying antibody, and anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies belong to myasthenia. Early aggressive treatment may reduce calcinosis. Skin and subcutaneous imaging can document its extent.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man on simvastatin has diffuse myalgias but normal strength and a normal creatine kinase. His thyroid tests and vitamin D are normal. What is the most reasonable approach?
options: Start prednisone and send biopsy immediately
Stop the statin and, after symptoms clear, rechallenge with a lower dose or a different statin
items.explanation: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are common, and without weakness or raised creatine kinase they are managed by stopping the drug, correcting contributors such as hypothyroidism or low vitamin D, and cautiously rechallenging with a lower dose or a different agent. Steroids and biopsy are for an immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with persistent weakness, and dialysis is for rhabdomyolysis with renal failure, which is absent here.

items.stem: A newborn is noted at 18 hours of age to have a weak cry, poor suck, and mild facial weakness. The mother has acetylcholine receptor antibody positive myasthenia gravis. Which statement best describes the expected course?
options: Progressive weakness that follows a sibling pattern of congenital myasthenia
Transient weakness from transplacental antibodies that resolves over days to weeks
Weakness that begins only after the first month of life
items.explanation: Neonatal myasthenia results from passive transfer of maternal IgG antibodies across the placenta. Symptoms appear in the first days, can require supportive feeding or short pyridostigmine courses, and resolve as maternal antibody is cleared over several weeks. It is not permanent, is not a genetic congenital myasthenic syndrome (which persists and lacks maternal antibodies), and does not start after a delay of a month.

items.stem: A technologist performs motor nerve conduction studies in a patient suspected of Lambert-Eaton syndrome. Which finding on testing supports the diagnosis?
options: Normal CMAP with a decrement greater than 10 percent at 3 Hz only
Prolonged distal latencies with conduction block
Repetitive CMAPs after a single stimulus
Low amplitude CMAP with an increment of more than 100 percent after brief exercise or fast stimulation
items.explanation: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome the baseline compound muscle action potential is small, and either brief maximal exercise or high-frequency stimulation increases it markedly, with a doubling or more considered diagnostic. A decrement at low rate occurs in both disorders but is not specific. Conduction block and slowed latencies suggest demyelinating neuropathy, and repetitive discharges after one stimulus suggest anticholinesterase toxicity or slow-channel syndrome.

items.stem: A 45-year-old farmer recovers from an acute cholinergic crisis after organophosphate exposure. Three days later he develops weakness of neck flexion, proximal limbs, and respiratory muscles, with no excess secretions. What does this represent?
items.explanation: Intermediate syndrome appears one to four days after the acute cholinergic phase and causes proximal limb, neck flexor, cranial, and respiratory weakness from persistent synaptic dysfunction, often requiring ventilation. A repeat cholinergic crisis would show excess secretions and miosis. Delayed polyneuropathy begins one to three weeks later with distal sensorimotor symptoms, and botulism is excluded by the exposure history and timing.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance, proximal muscle cramping, stiffness, and a creatine kinase of 1,500 U/L. Reflexes show a delayed relaxation phase. What is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanation: Hypothyroid myopathy produces proximal weakness, cramps, stiffness, slowed reflex relaxation, and raised creatine kinase, and it improves with thyroid hormone replacement, which should be started carefully if cardiac disease is possible. Steroids or plasma exchange would be unnecessary immunosuppression, and carnitine supplementation applies to a carnitine deficiency, not an endocrine myopathy. Thyroid function should be checked in any unexplained high creatine kinase.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy develops fever of 40 degrees Celsius, masseter rigidity, and tachycardia within minutes of receiving succinylcholine and sevoflurane for an appendectomy. A familial central core disease is later suspected. What is the first-line treatment of the acute reaction?
items.explanation: Masseter rigidity and hyperthermia after volatile agents or succinylcholine indicate malignant hyperthermia, linked to RYR1 mutations in central core disease. Triggers are stopped immediately and dantrolene, a ryanodine receptor antagonist, is given with cooling and supportive care. Pyridostigmine would aggravate weakness, haloperidol is used for agitation, not hyperthermia from calcium release, and propranolol does not reverse the underlying process.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has slowly progressive proximal weakness, orthopnea, and a falling forced vital capacity that is worse when supine. Creatine kinase is mildly elevated and electromyography shows myotonic discharges in paraspinal muscles. What is the best confirmatory test?
options: Acid alpha-glucosidase activity assay, then genetic testing
Forearm ischemic exercise testing with serial lactate sampling
items.explanation: Late-onset Pompe disease causes limb-girdle weakness with early diaphragm involvement and can show myotonic or complex repetitive discharges in axial muscles. Acid alpha-glucosidase activity assay, followed by GAA mutation analysis, confirms the diagnosis, and enzyme replacement can stabilize function. Forearm exercise testing evaluates glycolytic defects such as McArdle, a junction study would not explain paraspinal discharges, and nerve biopsy is unrelated.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has muscle stiffness that is worst when he starts to walk after sitting and improves after a few steps. He has hypertrophied muscles, and his stiffness is not worsened by cold. His mother is similarly affected. Which medication is most appropriate if symptomatic treatment is needed?
items.explanation: Myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutation shows warm-up improvement of stiffness with repeated movement and muscle hypertrophy, and mexiletine, a sodium channel blocker, reduces myotonia. Acetazolamide is used for periodic paralysis, dantrolene for malignant hyperthermia, and pyridostigmine for junction disorders. Lack of cold sensitivity helps separate it from paramyotonia congenita. Many patients need no drug at all if symptoms are mild.

items.stem: A 6-year-old ambulatory boy with Duchenne muscular dystrophy is considered for a one-time adeno-associated viral vector delivering a micro-dystrophin gene. Which risk requires close monitoring after infusion?
items.explanation: Micro-dystrophin gene therapy uses a shortened dystrophin that fits within the vector, and viral vector infusion carries risks of immune-mediated reactions including myocarditis and acute liver injury, so liver tests and troponin are followed closely. Hypocalcemic tetany, peripheral neuropathy, and cataracts are not characteristic complications. Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to the vector can also exclude a patient.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman in myasthenic crisis needs rapid immunotherapy. She has selective IgA deficiency and previously had an anaphylactic reaction to intravenous immune globulin. Which treatment is the best choice?
options: Repeat intravenous immune globulin with antihistamine premedication
items.explanation: Plasma exchange and intravenous immune globulin are equivalent rapid options in crisis. Anaphylaxis to immune globulin in IgA deficiency, driven by anti-IgA antibodies, makes further infusion unsafe, and premedication does not remove that risk. Azathioprine takes months to work and rituximab acts over weeks, so neither can reverse a crisis. Exchange removes antibody quickly and avoids the allergen.

items.stem: During 3 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation in a patient with generalized myasthenia gravis, a decrement of 20 percent is seen at rest. The test is repeated three minutes after one minute of maximal exercise. What is the expected result?
options: The decrement disappears for a further ten minutes
The decrement turns into an increment greater than 100 percent
The first potential doubles in amplitude
The decrement is larger than at rest
items.explanation: In myasthenia, brief exercise causes transient post-activation facilitation, and the decrement improves for about a minute. Several minutes later, post-activation exhaustion appears and the decrement becomes greater than at baseline, which is a useful way to bring out a borderline result. A marked increment and a doubled first response are features of presynaptic disorders such as Lambert-Eaton syndrome and botulism.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has had six months of fluctuating drooping of the right eyelid and intermittent double vision that worsens toward evening. Placing an ice pack over the closed eyelid for two minutes clearly improves the ptosis. Which mechanism best explains this bedside finding?
options: Cooling increases the density of functional acetylcholine receptors at the endplate within minutes
Cooling reduces acetylcholinesterase activity and improves neuromuscular transmission
Cooling blocks presynaptic calcium channel antibodies
Cooling reduces circulating antibody titers locally
items.explanation: The ice pack test is a bedside screen for ocular myasthenia. Lower temperature slows acetylcholinesterase activity and prolongs acetylcholine action in the cleft, which briefly improves a transmission already limited by a reduced receptor reserve. Cooling does not create new receptors, does not alter presynaptic calcium channels (which are the target in Lambert-Eaton syndrome), and has no local effect on circulating antibody levels.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man of French-Canadian descent has progressive swallowing difficulty and bilateral ptosis, and his brother has similar symptoms. Which treatment is most likely to relieve his dysphagia?
items.explanation: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy is autosomal dominant, caused by a short GCN expansion in PABPN1, and presents in later life with ptosis and dysphagia. Cricopharyngeal myotomy can improve swallowing for selected patients. Pyridostigmine, immune globulin, and steroids are used for myasthenia gravis or inflammatory disease and do not alter the dystrophic process, which is the main distinction from myasthenia in an older patient with ptosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had limb-girdle weakness since adolescence, with mild ptosis and no fatigue pattern that correlates with activity. Receptor and MuSK antibodies are negative, and muscle biopsy shows small endplates. Her weakness worsens on pyridostigmine. A mutation in which gene is most likely?
items.explanation: DOK7 congenital myasthenic syndrome causes limb-girdle weakness with small, simplified endplates, and anticholinesterase drugs worsen it, with salbutamol or ephedrine and 3,4-diaminopyridine as the better options. CHRNE and RAPSN defects usually respond to pyridostigmine and are commonly seen with ocular and bulbar features in infancy. SCN4A encodes the muscle sodium channel and causes myotonia or periodic paralysis, not this picture.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man with refractory acetylcholine receptor antibody positive generalized myasthenia gravis is offered efgartigimod. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Blockade of the neonatal Fc receptor, which increases catabolism of IgG
Binding of complement component C5 to prevent its cleavage into active products
Depletion of CD20 positive B cells
Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in the cleft
items.explanation: Efgartigimod is an Fc fragment that blocks the neonatal Fc receptor, which normally recycles IgG, so pathogenic autoantibody levels fall faster. Eculizumab and ravulizumab bind C5, rituximab depletes CD20 positive cells, and pyridostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase. Knowing the target explains the expected effect on total IgG and the infection risk profile of each class. This also explains why total IgG falls.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has proximal thigh weakness, muscle pain, early cataracts, and mild myotonia. Her mother was affected later in life and no congenital form has appeared in the family. Which condition is most likely?
options: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 with a CTG expansion in the DMPK gene
Myotonic dystrophy type 2 with a CCTG expansion in CNBP
items.explanation: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 produces proximal rather than distal weakness, prominent myalgia, cataracts, and milder myotonia, with a CCTG expansion in CNBP and no congenital form. Type 1 usually shows distal weakness, facial involvement, and congenital disease. Oculopharyngeal dystrophy features ptosis and dysphagia, and paramyotonia congenita is a sodium channelopathy with cold-induced myotonia without limb atrophy.

items.stem: A 9-month-old infant has profound hypotonia, a weak cry, and muscle biopsy showing rod-shaped inclusions on Gomori trichrome staining. Which diagnosis is most likely?
items.explanation: Nemaline rods are Z-disc derived inclusions that stain red on Gomori trichrome and define nemaline myopathy, most often caused by ACTA1 or NEB mutations. Central core disease shows well-demarcated cores lacking oxidative enzyme activity, centronuclear myopathy shows central nuclei, and mitochondrial myopathy shows ragged red fibers, so the stain pattern distinguishes the congenital myopathies. Genetic testing then confirms the specific gene.

items.stem: A 16-year-old boy has fixed elbow contractures, a rigid spine, and humeroperoneal weakness. His father required a pacemaker at age 35 and an uncle died suddenly. Genetic testing shows a LMNA mutation. What is the most important management priority?
options: Regular cardiac rhythm monitoring with early consideration of an implantable defibrillator
Daily high-dose corticosteroids to preserve strength
Surgery to release all contractures before adulthood
items.explanation: Emery-Dreifuss dystrophy due to LMNA mutation carries a high risk of atrial arrhythmias, conduction block, and sudden death that is independent of skeletal weakness, so lifelong rhythm surveillance and early device therapy, often a defibrillator because of malignant arrhythmias, are the priority. Steroids are not beneficial, contracture release does not alter survival, and cataracts are not a feature of this disorder.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has fatigable bulbar weakness, but acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies are negative and repetitive stimulation is normal. Which electrodiagnostic study has the highest sensitivity for a neuromuscular junction disorder in this setting?
options: Motor conduction velocity testing of the median nerve and the ulnar nerve
items.explanation: Single-fiber EMG is the most sensitive test for junction transmission failure, with abnormal jitter in most myasthenia patients even when repetitive stimulation is normal, though it is not specific. Conduction velocity assesses nerve myelin, fibrillation potentials point to denervation or necrotizing myopathy, and high-frequency stimulation is used mainly to look for an increment in presynaptic disorders.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has confirmed Lambert-Eaton syndrome with P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies. Imaging has not revealed a tumor yet. Which medication provides the best initial symptomatic improvement?
items.explanation: Amifampridine blocks presynaptic potassium channels, prolongs depolarization, and increases calcium entry and acetylcholine release, which improves strength and autonomic symptoms. Atropine would worsen dry mouth, dantrolene reduces muscle contraction and would aggravate weakness, and edrophonium has too short an effect to serve as maintenance. Tumor search and immunotherapy are added in parallel but do not replace symptomatic treatment.
